prompt: Write a short blog post about why services should be built around users, not around the org chart. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
# Build Services Around Users, Not the Org Chart

Every organization has a shape. There are teams, departments, reporting lines, and budget owners. That shape is useful for managing people. It is a terrible blueprint for designing services.

Yet it's how many services end up built. The billing team owns the invoice screen. The support team owns the help center. The onboarding team owns the welcome flow. Each piece works, and each team hits its own goals. Then a customer tries to fix a wrong charge and gets bounced across three systems, three tones of voice, and three different forms asking for the same account number.

Users don't see your org chart. They see a single company and a single problem they're trying to solve. When the structure of your service mirrors your internal structure, you push the cost of that complexity onto the people least equipped to absorb it.

This is the pattern Conway's Law describes: organizations design systems that copy their own communication structures. The result isn't malice or laziness. It's gravity. The easiest thing to build is whatever fits inside one team's remit, so that's what gets built.

## Start from the journey

Building around users means starting with what someone is trying to get done: move house, dispute a charge, renew a license. These tasks almost never respect departmental lines. A person changing their address doesn't think of it as three separate updates to three separate systems. They think of it as one thing.

Map that journey end to end, including the parts that happen outside your product, such as the phone call, the email, or the paper form. Gaps and handoffs show up quickly, and almost all of them sit at team boundaries.

## Make someone own the whole thing

Journeys fall apart when nobody owns them. Give a person or a team responsibility for the outcome, not just a component. Measure success by whether users complete their task, not by whether each team shipped its feature.

This often means cross-functional teams that bring design, engineering, policy, and operations together around a user need. It also means being willing to change internal processes so the service can be simple, rather than hiding the complexity behind a nicer interface.

## The payoff

Services built around users are easier to learn, cheaper to support, and harder to break. Fewer handoffs mean fewer places for things to go wrong. Fewer duplicate forms mean fewer errors to correct later.

You'll never fully escape the org chart. People still need managers and budgets need owners. The goal is to stop letting it decide what users experience. Draw the service first. Then organize the teams to deliver it.
